name: Mountain Climbers
tierNote: Safety tier C (content.md 5.1: not in the A or B lists); census.json difficulty tier 3.

claims.text: Mountain climbers are a moving plank: from a raised push-up position the feet are brought forward one at a time toward the chest.

quotes.text: Mountain climbers are like a moving plank: You start in a raised push-up position and hop your feet forward, one at a time, toward your chest.

claims.text: Hands go directly under the shoulders with the arms straight.

quotes.text: Start on your hands and knees with your arms straight and hands placed directly under your shoulders.

claims.text: The body forms a straight line from the back of the head to the heels, on hands and toes.

quotes.text: Extend your legs back behind you, supporting your body on your hands and toes. Your body should form a straight line from the back of your head to your heels (like a regular, raised push-up position or plank).

claims.text: Bring one foot toward the chest, then switch legs quickly as if running, without letting the hips hike up.

quotes.text: From here, hop one foot toward your chest, and then quickly switch legs, as if you're running. Try not to let your hips hike up as you move.

claims.text: Keep the plank position while the legs alternate.

quotes.text: Maintain that plank position as you continue to alternate legs.

claims.text: Shifting the weight backward makes balance harder; keep the shoulders over the wrists and press slightly forward.

quotes.text: Weight shifting backward. Shifting your weight backward can reduce some of the pressure on your arms and core, but it can also make it tougher to maintain balance and stability.
A helpful adjustment here is to keep your shoulders directly over your wrists and imagine pressing slightly forward.

claims.text: Bouncing on the toes adds impact; glide the knees forward with smooth steps instead.

quotes.text: Bouncing on your toes. Some people find themselves bouncing on their toes as they drive their knees forward. This can add extra impact, especially for beginners, which might make it harder to keep the movement controlled.
To adjust, focus on moving with smooth, intentional steps, almost as if you’re gliding your knees forward rather than bouncing.

claims.text: Some back rounding is natural with fatigue; if it becomes excessive, draw the shoulders down and back and engage the core.

quotes.text: Some rounding in your back is natural, especially as you start to fatigue. If you feel your back rounding excessively, try focusing on drawing your shoulders down and back, which supports a neutral spine position.
Engaging your core helps to keep your torso steady, which can help you feel stronger and less strained throughout the movement.

claims.text: Easier versions: step instead of hopping, put the hands on a sturdy bench or step, or shorten the knee drive.

quotes.text: Step, instead of jump. Rather than jumping to switch legs, step one foot forward, then step it back, and repeat with the other leg.
Place your hands on an elevated surface, like a sturdy bench or step. This reduces the load on your arms and core, making the exercise less intense than starting from the floor.
Instead of bringing your knee all the way to your chest, only bring it halfway or as far as is comfortable.

claims.text: Progression: a faster pace raises the cardio and core demand.

quotes.text: Pick up the pace. Do the movement at a faster pace to increase the cardio intensity. This will also challenge your core and legs to move quickly and efficiently.

claims.text: You may feel the core, shoulders and arms, and the glutes, thighs and hips working; the hip flexors lift the legs.

quotes.text: As you do each rep, you might feel your core, shoulder, and arm muscles working, as well as your butt, thighs, and hips.
quotes.where: To do mountain climbers, after step 4

quotes.text: Hip flexors. These muscles help you flex at the hip (thus the name) when you walk and do other activities that require lifting your legs.
Rectus abdominis. This sheet of muscle — often called the "six-pack" muscle — spans the front of your abdomen

claims.text: Planks and push-ups load the wrist bent back; in patients with pain on the back of the wrist in this position, MRI found an abnormality in 84 %. This is a patient series, not a risk estimate for healthy exercisers.

quotes.text: Many exercise disciplines incorporate upper extremity weight-bearing exercises in an extended wrist posture, for example push-ups, plank position, and various yoga and Pilates poses.
MRI demonstrated an identifiable dorsal abnormality in 84% of patients with dorsal wrist pain associated with weight bearing on the extended wrist.

claims.text: Programmed by time: beginners 2–3 sets of 15 seconds on, 15 off; intermediate 3–4 sets of 20 on, 20 off; well conditioned 4–5 sets of 30 on, 30 off.

quotes.text: Mountain climbers are usually programmed by time rather than reps. Beginners should start with 2 to 3 sets of 15 seconds of work and 15 seconds of rest, which totals about 1 to 2 minutes.
quotes.where: FAQ: How many mountain climbers should I do?

quotes.text: At intermediate level, use 3 to 4 sets of 20 seconds on and 20 seconds off, and if you are well conditioned, 4 to 5 sets of 30 seconds on and 30 seconds off.
quotes.where: FAQ: How many mountain climbers should I do?

claims.text: For strength, 2–3 sets of 10–15 slow, controlled reps (slow is better for beginners); for HIIT, 6–8 rounds of 20 seconds fast with 10 seconds rest.

quotes.text: As part of an overall program focusing on muscular strength and conditioning, complete 2–3 sets of 10–15 slow and controlled repetitions.
As part of a cardiovascular program with a HIIT focus, complete 6–8 rounds of fast mountain climbers for 20 seconds, with a 10-second rest in between.
They can also be performed at a slow, controlled tempo, which is better for beginners.

claims.text: Progress by lengthening the interval before adding sets, and end the set as soon as the hips start bouncing rather than pushing to the clock.

quotes.text: Progress by extending the interval before adding sets, and end the set as soon as your hips start bouncing rather than pushing to the clock.

plate.viewWhy: The knee drive toward the chest (c4), the straight head-to-heel line (c3) and the hands-under-shoulders stack (c2, c6) are sagittal; the hip-hike fault reads from the side.
plate.frames: Cycle convention (architecture section 1): one half-cycle, from the high plank to one knee driven toward the chest; Trace follows the driving knee; tempo covers one cycle.
plate.start: High plank on hands and toes, arms straight, hands under the shoulders (c2), straight line from the back of the head to the heels (c3).
plate.end: One knee driven toward the chest, the other leg still straight behind, hips not hiked (c4), shoulders still over the wrists (c6).

checkpoints.label: Hands under shoulders
checkpoints.what: Arms straight, hands directly under the shoulders, shoulders over the wrists.

checkpoints.label: Straight line
checkpoints.what: Head to heels in one line, as in a plank.

checkpoints.label: Knee to chest
checkpoints.what: One foot comes forward toward the chest, then the legs switch.

mistake.what: Hips hike up as the knee drives forward.
mistake.why: The anchor's own how-to step warns against it (c4); it breaks the plank line the movement depends on (c3, c5).
mistake.rankNote: No source ranks faults by frequency. Hinge Health's common-adjustments list also names bouncing, weight shifting backward and back rounding (c6-c8); weight shifting back is also drawable and suits the layers.

tells.text: Hips stay level as legs switch

tempo.text: Default (beginner): 2-3 sets of 15 s on, 15 s off (c13), switching legs quickly, as if running (c4); slow and controlled suits beginners (c14). Progressions: 20 s on/20 s off, then 30 s on/30 s off, lengthening the interval before adding sets; end the set when the hips start bouncing (c13, c15). High-intensity option only: 6-8 rounds of 20 s fast, 10 s rest (c14). No source gives steps per second.

grip.wrist: Wrist bent back under body weight (as in planks and push-ups, c12).
grip.note: No source found on finger spread, weight through the heel of the hand, or whether fists or push-up handles help a sore wrist.

setup.step: Start on hands and knees, arms straight, hands under your shoulders.
Step your legs back onto your toes; body in one straight line.
Bring one foot toward your chest, then switch legs quickly.
Keep the plank position the whole time.

posture.point: Straight line from head to heels.

handlingMistakes.fix: Keep the plank line; slow down or step instead of hopping.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Weight shifts back toward the feet.
handlingMistakes.fix: Shoulders over wrists, press slightly forward.
Glide the knees forward with smooth steps.

rows.means: The hip flexors lifting the legs.

rows.where: Pain on the back of the wrist
rows.fixNote: The shared wrist box covers what to do next. Hands on a bench or step (c9) only means less load on the arms and core; no source says it relieves the wrist, so it is not offered as a wrist fix.

risks.risk: Pain on the back of the wrist in the loaded, bent-back position.
Bouncing adds impact and costs control.

zooms.right: Palm flat, hand directly under the shoulder.
zooms.wrong: Hands ahead of the shoulders, weight shifted back.

zooms.right: Hips level with the head-to-heel line.
zooms.wrong: Hips hiked up as the knee drives.

libraryDiff.why: Library: core primary; hip_flexors and abs secondary. Hinge Health lists hip flexors and rectus abdominis among the muscles worked (c11), which matches. It also lists chest, deltoids, triceps, glutes and quads, but it is a coaching list with no EMG, so no change is proposed.

anchorNote: Hinge Health (physical therapists) mountain climbers page read in full. No ACE, NSCA or ACSM mountain climber page was reachable, and PubMed has no technique or EMG study of the exercise (search 2026-09-30: 3 hits for mountain climber AND EMG, none relevant).
unsourced: Cadence (steps per second); work and rest times are now sourced (c13, c14).
Finger spread and weight through the heel of the hand (palm-flat archetype).
Whether fists or push-up handles help a sore wrist.
Where the driving foot lands (toe tap vs floating).
notes: Tempo research 2026-10-02 (LIB-3 H2, pilot A #109): c13 (Julie Lohre) and c14 (Healthline) add timed work and rest; no source gives a cadence.

W1 fix round 2026-10-03: F05/R-W1-2 tempo default is the beginner row (2-3 × 15 s on/15 s off, c13); 20/20 and 30/30 are progressions; 20/10 is labelled as the high-intensity option (c14). c15 adds Lohre's progression and stop cue; loadProgression added from c13 and c15.

loadProgression.text: Start with 2-3 sets of 15 seconds on, 15 off; lengthen the interval before adding sets; stop the set when your hips start bouncing.
